title: Mindfulness of the body
hookLine: like a heavy stone ball thrown on wet clay, or a full water jar tipped

lines: AFTER THE MEAL, IN THE HALL.
THE BUDDHA ASKS: WHAT'S THE TALK?
A STONE BALL. WET CLAY. A WATER JAR.
cards: It's after the meal, and a group of monks is sitting in the assembly hall, talking. It's wonderful, one of them says, how the Buddha calls mindfulness of the body a thing of great fruit.
They're still talking when the Buddha walks in and asks what they were discussing. So he tells them himself.
The hundred and nineteenth discourse is that answer, and near its end come pictures you can almost hold: a stone ball, a lump of wet clay, a water jar on a stand.

teach.b: Mindfulness of the body, kayagatasati, starts simply. Knowing the breath. Knowing the posture: walking, standing, sitting, lying down.
Acting with full awareness, whether you're stretching an arm or chewing food. Then reviewing the body's parts, its elements, its mortality.
Then the absorptions, with pictures: rapture and ease soaking through the body like water kneaded into bath powder, until no part is dry. Then the Buddha says something large.

Whoever has developed mindfulness of the body has within it all the good states that lead to true knowledge, the way someone who pictures the great ocean includes every river that runs into it. Now the images.

teach.h: STONE BALL OR BALL OF STRING
teach.b: If you haven't developed it, it's like throwing a heavy stone ball onto a mound of wet clay: it sinks right in. That's how Mara, the tempter, finds a way in. Or like an empty water jar: anyone can pour water into it.
But if you have developed it, it's like a light ball of string thrown at a door of solid wood. It bounces off.

teach.h: THE FULL JAR, TIPPED AT WILL
teach.b: Or a jar already full to the brim: there's no room to pour anything in. And tip a full jar on its stand, and the water flows out wherever you choose: the mind can turn toward any of the higher knowledges.
The text lists ten benefits, from enduring heat, cold and harsh words to freedom itself.
All starting from a body you already have.

how: Theravada and other Buddhist teachers often begin meditation with awareness of the body, including breath, posture and walking meditation, and some monastics contemplate the parts of the body as part of their training.

o: the belief that the body is the true self
a set of exercises for keeping the body fit
mindfulness of the body: breath, posture, action

games.q: the body, in pictures: tap the pairs.

s: MN 119 begins with monks talking after their meal
they're praising mindfulness of the body when the Buddha comes in and asks what they're discussing.
in the simile, the heavy stone ball bounces off the wet clay
it sinks right in: that's the undeveloped mind. the light ball of string bounces off solid wood.
the discourse lists ten benefits of mindfulness of the body
among them enduring heat, cold and harsh words, and in the end, freedom.

games.q: a jar is full to the brim. someone comes to pour more water in. what happens, in the Buddha's picture?
o: there's no room, so it can't be poured in.
games.why: the full jar has no room. so the mind filled with body mindfulness gives distraction no place to enter.

practice: Let gravity have you, and feel where you meet the chair or the floor: the pressure under your thighs, your feet, your hands resting. You aren't trying to relax, just to know you're here, sitting.
When the mind drifts, come back to weight and contact, like a full jar with no room for much else.

wordCard.voice: Kayagatasati. Mindfulness of the body: knowing breath, posture and action, so the mind is like a full jar that nothing can pour into.

orig.note: Pali kayagatasati: mindfulness directed to the body. the title of MN 119.

carryVoice: Your line: the body is enough. A full jar leaves no room for anything else. Until tomorrow.
